oil.summary: Crude closed a turbulent June on a mixed note: WTI slipped 1.02% to $70.03/bbl while Brent edged up 0.30% to $73.37, though both contracts are nursing losses of roughly 20% on the month — the steepest monthly sell-off in recent memory. RBOB gasoline was the session's standout laggard, cratering 5.17%. The bearish macro backdrop is dominated by Morgan Stanley cutting its Brent forecast to $75/bbl, citing an expected acceleration of supply as Hormuz flows normalise, while the EIA reported U.S. crude output hitting a record 13.934 mb/d. Partially offsetting that, the API logged a 6.072 mb/d inventory draw and Ukraine's drone campaign against Russian refineries deepened, with Putin publicly acknowledging domestic fuel shortages for the first time. A contrarian piece today argued that an Iranian supply crunch could paradoxically push prices below $40, complicating the near-term outlook.
drivers: Record U.S. crude production at 13.934 mb/d and Morgan Stanley's $75/bbl Brent forecast cut reinforce oversupply narrative after a 20% monthly price collapse
Strait of Hormuz tension persists — renewed U.S.-Iran strikes keep summer volatility elevated even as flows partially resume, with options markets pricing no OPEC production increase
Ukraine drone strikes ignite multiple Russian refineries; Putin admits domestic fuel shortages, injecting a geopolitical supply-disruption premium into an otherwise bearish tape

gas.summary: Natural gas firmed on both sides of the Atlantic on the final day of June. Henry Hub gained 2.39% to $3.257/MMBtu, extending a 3.50% weekly advance, while TTF rose 2.61% to €43.675/MWh, also up nearly 4% on the week. The positive session comes despite both benchmarks sitting in the red on a monthly basis. The primary headline catalyst is Shell's long-term demand outlook projecting a 65% surge in global LNG demand by 2050, led by South and Southeast Asia — Thailand's state-owned PTT is already in early-stage talks to invest directly in U.S. LNG export projects to lock in long-term supply. Hormuz tensions remain a secondary watch item given the strait's importance to LNG transit, though flows have continued so far.
drivers: Shell projects 65% global LNG demand growth by 2050, anchored by Asian appetite, supporting longer-dated sentiment
Thailand's PTT in talks to invest in U.S. LNG export projects, reflecting buyers' urgency to secure supply amid tightening long-term availability
Hormuz flows continuing despite geopolitical stress, limiting acute supply-disruption premium, but remaining a live tail risk for the sector

power.summary: EU carbon allowances (EUA) added 1.35% to $75.865/EUA, recovering modestly after a flat week and building on a marginal 1.46% monthly gain — a notable contrast to the sharp sell-offs in oil. The session lacked dedicated power-sector headlines, so the driver set is thin. Geopolitically, Iran's $6 billion asset release from Qatar and the partial reopening of the Strait of Hormuz are reshaping Gulf energy dynamics in ways that could reduce LNG supply-risk premia, indirectly weighing on gas-linked power costs. The UK announced nearly 300 new sanctions targeting Russia's Transneft, adding further stress to Russian energy export infrastructure. China's latest five-year plan confirms continued parallel investment in both coal and solar/wind, signalling no near-term reduction in Chinese carbon intensity.
drivers: EUA prices hold above $75 with modest daily and monthly gains, suggesting carbon market participants are not yet pricing in a sharp demand destruction scenario despite the oil rout
UK sanctions on Transneft and ongoing Russian refinery disruptions tighten European energy supply chains, providing indirect floor support for continental gas and power prices
China's five-year plan confirms dual coal-and-renewables expansion strategy, limiting expectations of a near-term structural reduction in global carbon emissions
